profile.headline: Software Developer | AI, ERP & Internal Tools for Manufacturing
profile.summary:
I started out as a chemist. Somewhere along the way I realized I enjoyed building the tools more than running the experiments, and I've been writing software ever since. The lab habits stuck: understand the system before you touch it, measure instead of guessing, and don't call it done until it's verified.

I build and run internal software for a manufacturing company: warehouse management, dispatch scheduling, purchasing, kitting, production analytics, all integrated with our ERP (Aptean Made2Manage). Manufacturing has a reputation for being slow to adopt new technology, and I've made it my job to be the counterexample, using AI and modern tooling to continuously improve how we work.

I learned to code before AI could write it, and that matters more now, not less. I integrate AI across the entire pipeline, from design through implementation, review, and monitoring, and it has made me measurably faster. The fundamentals are what make that speed safe: knowing what's worth building, designing systems that match how the shop floor actually works, standing up the infrastructure and cloud services underneath (AWS, SQL Server, MySQL, Nginx), and verifying that what ships holds up in production. Python and Rust, end to end, from the database to the DNS record.

The work I'm proudest of lately is the AI data layer I designed and run for the company: a fleet of MCP servers that let coworkers pull live ERP data, look up jobs, parts, and orders, or kick off reports just by asking an AI assistant. No setup, no SQL, no tickets to me. What they experience as "it just answers" is the part I own: which tools exist and how they compose, the curated query recipes that encode years of tribal knowledge about our data, the safety design (read-only by default, confirm-gated writes, per-user identity and audit logging), and the error messages that coach the AI back on track instead of dead-ending. None of it is visible when it works, which is the point.

I also ship AI systems that run unattended: an autonomous agent that researches vendor pricing every morning and emails a summary, AI-triaged log monitoring, vision pipelines that extract structured data from scanned production documents. The bar is the same as for everything else: it has to still be working, quietly, six months later.
What I enjoy most is full ownership: spot a problem on the floor, design the fix, ship it, keep it running.

I contribute to open source and I'm always glad to connect over internal tooling, manufacturing software, or applied AI
